source_document.body:
Photo: Tesla
Elon Musk now says Tesla will keep building the Cybertruck “through the end of summer 2027” to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” That buys the electric pickup roughly two to three more months, five days after Tesla first announced it was killing it.
The reprieve lands as a growing number of Tesla’s own fans push back on the decision, and on what it says about Tesla’s future as a company that sells cars to people.
Three end dates in five days
On November 6, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas “around the middle of next year” to make room for Cybercab. On November 9, he wrote the line would shut “in about 8 months” and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.” Now it’s the end of summer.
In order to work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog, production will be extended through the end of summer 2027 — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 11, 2026
The reasons have moved around just as much. First it was factory space, then “a very limited number of smart, dedicated people,” then the “opportunity cost” of the truck’s complexity. We went through each of them: Tesla is ending the Cybertruck as sales stall at about 10% of plan , Musk’s demand claim doesn’t survive the numbers , and Musk admitted Tesla doesn’t have the talent to run more than one vehicle program .
Advertisement - scroll for more content
And the “backlog” is one Tesla built itself. Before the announcement, the truck was selling at a pace of roughly 30,000 units a year, about 10% of the 250,000 Tesla planned for, on a line with over 125,000 units of installed capacity. Telling people the truck is going away creates a last-call rush. That’s not demand Tesla was missing before.
Tesla also raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% the same day and paused orders for the base Dual Motor. The cheapest Cybertruck you can order is now $92,490, up from $69,990 in early August.
Some of the people in that backlog have been waiting a while. Several cheering in Musk’s replies say they’re still waiting on the $59,990 Cybertruck Tesla sold for “10 days only” in February. One asked whether Tesla will prioritize Premium and Cyberbeast orders over theirs. Musk didn’t answer.
Tesla fans are asking the right question
The most telling replies weren’t about the truck. Chuck Cook, one of the best-known FSD testers in the Tesla community, quote-tweeted Musk asking him to “change your mind,” adding: “Cybercab won’t haul my bees.”
Another longtime Tesla supporter, Phil Trubey, asked for “a vehicle roadmap post end of summer 2027,” followed by: “Will Tesla make any other vehicle?”
That’s the right question, and Tesla hasn’t announced a single new consumer vehicle to answer it. Tesla started 2026 with five consumer vehicle programs: Model S, Model X, Model 3, Model Y, and Cybertruck. It ended Model S and Model X production in the spring, citing “autonomy.” The Cybertruck goes next. By fall 2027, Tesla’s consumer lineup will be the Model 3 and Model Y, two vehicles that launched in 2017 and 2020.
Tesla’s answer to the affordable car it promised for years was stripped-down “Standard” versions of those same two vehicles. In China, its second-biggest market, Tesla turned Giga Shanghai into an export hub, and domestic retail sales crashed 66% in October to the lowest level in over four years .
Even Unplugged Performance, the biggest Tesla tuner around, offered to take the Cybertruck line off Tesla’s hands and pay a license fee. People want this truck built. Tesla doesn’t.
Electrek’s Take
We’ve been warning about this for years, and for years we got called haters for it.
The pattern has been clear since Tesla swapped its affordable car plans for Robotaxi in 2024. No new consumer platform. Model S and X killed “for autonomy.” Cybertruck killed “for Cybercab.” A Roadster pitched as a thruster stunt nine years after its unveiling. Every product decision points away from selling cars to people and toward robotaxis and Optimus, two businesses that don’t generate meaningful revenue today.
Top comment by bruce Mauhar
Liked by 6 people
I am beginning to suspect that Elon does not always tell the truth.
As long as we have an economic climate that allows massive amounts of money to be made off of speculation as opposed to actual product, future bots and robotaxis have a great deal of value whether they actually become viable or not.
View all comments
A two-to-three-month extension doesn’t change any of that. It’s a gesture to the loudest part of the fan base, and it happens to let Tesla sell a few thousand more trucks at prices up to 10% higher than last week. Fine. But the people who bought into Tesla’s mission to accelerate the world’s transition to sustainable energy are now realizing that mission was quietly rewritten, and the word “sustainable” didn’t make the cut.
Tesla is becoming a company that sells two aging EVs to fund a bet on autonomy. That might work out for shareholders. We have our doubts, given Tesla is still behind Waymo by every public metric. But it’s a lot less exciting for the people who wanted the next great Tesla car.
The question for fans now: when the Model 3 and Model Y get their own “opportunity cost” post on X, will anyone actually be surprised?
If you’re buying an EV, Cybertruck or not, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. And with lease and PPA options, you can do it with zero upfront cost and start saving immediately. If you want to find the best deal, check out EnergySage . Gold Fields vice-president of environment and community relations in Canada Andréanne Boisvert (L) chats with TNM's Western Editor, Henry Lazenby.
Posted By: Henry Lazenby November 11, 2026
Gold Fields (JSE, NYSE: GFI) can begin preparing its Windfall gold project in Quebec for construction after securing provincial environmental approval, with a final investment decision still ahead.
Early work will include civil works and assembling a camp to house construction workers, Andréanne Boisvert, Gold Fields vice-president of environment and community relations in Canada, told The Northern Miner last week at Xplor in Montreal. Windfall is about 415 km northwest of Quebec City.
“Following the expiration of our bulk sample permit in August, we had slowed down our activities, and so now we can restart our underground activities,” Boisvert said. “With this in hand, we can now apply to all our secondary permits that are required for construction.”
Gold Fields also plans deeper drilling to convert resources into reserves and test whether it can extend the roughly 10-year mine plan, Boisvert said.
Watch below the full interview with The Miner’s Western Editor, Henry Lazenby:

Two U.S. Army UH-60 Black Hawk helicopters assigned to the 4th Combat Aviation Brigade, 4th Infantry Division, take off for flight over the Rocky Mountains during Ivy Sting VII on Fort Carson, Colorado, Oct. 27, 2026. The aircraft supported a senior aviation branch leadership visit highlighting the division's progress in integrating Next Generation Command and Control (NGC2) capabilities and preparing aviation formations for the evolving demands of multidomain operations. (U.S. Army photo by Sgt. Doniel Kennedy)
The Army’s Next Generation Command and Control (NGC2) initiative aims to build a unified data infrastructure that can speed up data collection, management, analysis and decision-making not only for its commanders and troops in the field, but also with partners, allies and other branches of the US military.
Breaking Defense spoke with Josh Wallin, Defense Program fellow at the Center for a New American Security, on what needs NGC2 will meet, the data infrastructure necessary to implement NGC2 and how it will help speed up the response to constantly changing threats on the battlefield.
Breaking Defense: What is the threat scenario driving the need for NGC2?
Wallin: There are a few different pieces of this. One is the recognition of just how important the EM spectrum is, how important emissions are and the degree to which we’re seeing jamming and interference and tracking emissions in Ukraine by the Russians.
Josh Wallin, Defense Program fellow, Center for a New American Security
Another is recognizing the fact that when we’re going against a more capable adversary. In an Indo-Pacific scenario, there’s just a much greater concern about what they can do to mess with communications, mess with data links between forces in the Army specifically.
Another piece is thinking about the distances that you’re dealing with. In the GWOT (Global War on Terror) era, certainly in Iran now or even in Ukraine, we haven’t faced the potential distances we would in the Pacific, and recognizing that you’re trying to connect a bunch of systems that may be located potentially thousands of miles apart from each other.
If we look at how the Army has to operate in the Pacific, it’s not just a distance issue. It’s also a network infrastructure issue.
It’s certainly an infrastructure issue. For at least the last few decades we haven’t really come in direct contact with an adversary that’s going to be targeting the spectrum quite so much. That’s important to be preparing for.
On the infrastructure piece, yes, there is commercial infrastructure that can support things. It’s not that that infrastructure doesn’t necessarily exist at all in the Pacific. I’m not an expert on how all of the Starlink satellites, as an example, have been distributed, but if you had terminals in the Pacific, my presumption is that you would probably still have connectivity in that way. Obviously you’re going to be less able to rely on commercial cellular infrastructure if that’s something you want to be using.
A big component of that is going to also end up being bandwidth. One of the things that the Army is seeing in Ukraine right now is the volume of data, of transmissions that are going out, and especially with all of these distributed operating concepts that the Army, Navy, Air Force are all looking at. There’s a recognition of the fact that you’re going to have to constantly be passing data between a bunch of different nodes to keep them synchronized. So a bunch of different deployed forces, to keep them in sync, you’re going to have less of this concept of centralization or mass in particular locations where it may be much easier to pass information.
What will NGC2 change for the Army at the mission level?
The cross-functional piece that I was alluding to before, to this idea that we should be able to connect systems across different functions with a recognition that data from one – what would have been stovepiped – may be valuable to another one.
There’s a recognition, in Ukraine as an example, that the targeting cycle is very fast. We might be talking on the order of minutes from acquisition to servicing a target. One goal is speeding things up, having that cross functional data that you can take advantage of.
Another piece is even more basic than that when you’re talking within particular functions. For air defense, when we look at systems like Patriot and THAAD, it’s a recent development that those systems are able to talk to and cue each other, that a THAAD radar is able to control a Patriot interceptor.
There is a general recognition of the fact that if we’re going to look at these layered defense concepts, you can’t have stovepiped systems that are acting completely on their own. It’s, one, super inefficient. Two, given the volume of threats we may be facing, it simply may lead to cases in which you can’t match the incoming threat because you’re not able to move information quickly enough and coordinate across units.
Military vehicles are staged outside the Mission Training Center during Ivy Sting 7 at Fort Carson, Colorado, Oct. 26, 2026. The exercise brought Soldiers and industry partners together to evaluate Next Generation Command and Control (NGC2) capabilities and improve battlefield coordination. (U.S. Army photo by Sgt. Cecilia Jasinski)
We have seen new threats emerging and changing rapidly. How will NGC2 help the Army adapt to that?
NGC2 seems focused on trying to modularize things as much as possible, trying to separate out those hardware pieces. How do we actually have data links? What cable is connected to what radio which is transmitting to which satellite? Separating that from the actual compute infrastructure you need, separating that from the data infrastructure you need.
They’re trying to separate out the software that manages all of your data. An application layer is going to sit on top of that, which is what soldiers are actually tapping into for their particular roles. The idea is if an adversary has adapted a novel way to jam or target or track some of your infrastructure, such as terminals for satellites, you would be able to quickly swap that out for some less vulnerable piece of hardware without having to change all of the things that sit above that.
There are staggering amounts of data being collected. How can that data be managed and used effectively?
The Army is pushing for this centralization of data across functions. Previously we had stovepiped systems where air-defense defense systems may have their own data and communication infrastructure. Logistics might have a separate one. Fires might have a separate one. The idea is that if we can unify all of that data, maybe we can usefully look at correlation across different data sources for different concerns.
If we think about something like logistics, we’re having all these conversations about just-in-time logistics and being able to manage distributed operations. You may want information about ongoing operations and the threat picture. You might want to be connected into intelligence directly. Unifying the data is one piece of that, being able to draw interesting conclusions from how data for different functions might relate to each other.
On the analytical piece, the buzzword continues to be artificial intelligence (AI), the hope that you’ll be able to automatically analyze portions of this data to present it usefully and quickly to operators. A part of that is being able to automate what processes you can, such as using AI or other data analysis techniques to speed up some of the tasks that might be highly manual right now or be able to get a 60 percent solution on something that was 100 percent manual before, and then freeing up more operators’ time.
As NGC2 is built and implemented, how can the Army ensure that it meets not only today’s needs but future needs?
From a hardware perspective, because of the proliferation of larger amounts of compute, there’s a bit more wiggle room in terms of systems being able to do things long term. Because compute is shrinking so much, because it’s becoming more widespread, that gives a nice runway for long-term applications. Maybe compute won’t go as stale quite so quickly for the things that we’re talking about.
The other piece is the Army is very aware and they seem to be really focusing on this idea that they’re not acquiring software solutions or hardware solutions for decades. They’re not expecting that they’re going to be using these same systems 60 years from now. They are really trying to be able to adapt quickly.

source_document.body:
Drilling at the Troilus project site. Credit: Troilus Mining.
By: Northern Miner Staff November 11, 2026
Troilus Mining (TSX: TLG; US-OTC: CHXMF) has found gold in past-producing ground treated as waste at its namesake Quebec project, raising the prospect of improving the planned open-pit operation’s economics.
Hole 87-26-524 cut 34 metres at 1.29 grams gold per tonne from 207 metres depth, including 12 metres at 3.04 grams, Troilus said Wednesday . The results come from the Z87 hanging wall, beside the main mineralized zone. “We view the results positively, as they support potential resource conversion, lower strip ratios, improved early-year mill feed and future pit optimization,” Desjardins Capital Markets mining analyst Bryce Adams said Wednesday in a note. The exploration work comes as Troilus assembles financing for a redevelopment on the site of a former gold-copper mine. The federal assessment registry places the project about 170 km north of Chibougamau and 615 km north of Montreal. Converting waste to ore could reduce stripping and improve early mill feed. The results still need modelling, since the resource and reserve underlying September’s updated study exclude all 2026 drilling, Troilus said. “We are confident in our existing mine plan, but remain committed to continual improvement and evaluating opportunities to strengthen it,” CEO Justin Reid said.
Drilling gaps
Some historical drill core was never assayed, leaving gaps in the geological model. Troilus is testing those intervals and inferred material around the proposed pit. Estimated true thicknesses are 75%–90% of the reported drill lengths. September’s development update for the project envisaged a 26-year operation, with construction anticipated in 2027, first ore in September 2029 and commercial production in March 2030. Initial capital was estimated at about $1.43 billion (C$2 billion), Troilus said. Troilus received a credit-approved commitment for $850 million in debt from KfW IPEX-Bank and Société Générale in September. The package contemplated a further $250 million from Export Development Canada, subject to that lender’s final approvals, Troilus said at the time.
Shares of Troilus dropped 2.8% to C$1.56 Wednesday afternoon in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$880 million ($629 million). The stock has traded between C$1.20 and C$2.47 in the past year.

source_document.body:
Counter-Current Decantation (CCD) thickener tanks at Thacker Pass. ( Image courtesy of Lithium Americas. )
By: Staff Writer November 11, 2026
Lithium Americas (TSX, NYSE: LAC) has raised the estimate for the first stage of its Thacker Pass lithium project in Nevada by 31% to $3.83 billion (C$5.43 billion), citing higher labour, construction and logistics expenses.
The revised budget adds $895 million in capital costs and increases the funding requirement by about $995 million, the company said Wednesday. Mechanical completion remains targeted for late 2027, with commercial production expected in 2028.
“Thacker Pass is on track to deliver America’s largest fully integrated source of domestic battery-quality lithium carbonate, and we are building it at pace,” CEO Jonathan Evans said in a statement. “Phase 0ne is advancing toward peak construction activity by year end 2026, with mechanical completion targeted for late 2027.”
The financing plan would increase Lithium Americas’ stake in its joint venture with General Motors (NYSE: GM), giving the developer a larger interest as it contributes more capital. The ownership changes are still being finalized with GM and the US Department of Energy (DOE), the company said.
Labour drives increase
Labour and staffing account for $645 million of the increase, including $245 million for installing piping, steel and equipment. Higher craft wages and incentives, additional engineering and construction staff, and increased contractor wage rates make up the balance.
Tariffs and logistics add $100 million, while additional contingency accounts for $150 million. Estimated tariff exposure alone has fallen to about $60 million from the previously forecast $80 million to $100 million, the company said.
Lithium Americas now expects to spend $1.7 billion to $2 billion on the first stage in 2026, up from its previous forecast of $1.3 billion to $1.6 billion.
Thacker Pass, about 100 km northwest of Winnemucca in northern Nevada, is designed to produce 40,000 tonnes of battery-grade lithium carbonate annually in its first stage. It is among the projects advancing to expand US lithium supply .
Funding plan
Lithium Americas expects to address the additional funding requirement through a $650-million contribution to the joint venture, $315 million available in DOE loan reserve accounts and a $30-million reduction in required sustaining-capital reserves under a loan amendment signed Nov. 10.
The company held about $1.3 billion in cash and restricted cash at Sept. 30, including about $360 million at the joint venture. Those figures are preliminary and unaudited.
Lithium Americas shares traded 8.2% weaker at C$2.47 in Toronto mid-Wednesday, valuing the company at about C$897 million. The shares have traded between C$2.43 and C$9.47 over the past 12 months.

Kia became the first non-European brand to score a hat trick at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, Germany’s most prestigious auto awards.
Kia wins big at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards
The Korean automaker won a triple crown at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, with the EV2, K4 Sportswagon, and EV5 taking first in their class.
This is the first time a non-European brand has won three Golden Steering Wheel Awards in a single year in the prestigious award’s 50-year history.
The award is organized by AUTO BILD and BILD am SONNTAG with 90 new models nominated this year. Readers chose 27 finalists, three in each of the nine classes, which were then tested by a panel of celebrities and auto experts.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The judges tested the vehicles at the DEKRA-Lausitzring racetrack. Vehicles were judged on handling, comfort, ease of use, quality, and everyday practicality, as well as the sustainability and value they offer.
Kia won across three very different categories with the fully electric EV2 and EV5, alongside the gas-powered K4 Sportswagon.
From left to right: Barbara Schöneberger, German television presenter, Ho Sung Song, President and CEO of Kia Corporation, Christoph Eck-Schmidt, CEO of BILD Group (Source: Kia)
The EV2, Kia’s entry-level electric SUV, won the award for the “Best Car Under €30,000.” Developed specifically for Europe, the compact EV is only 4.06 meters long, but offers up to 403 liters of cargo space.
It also offers a WLTP driving range of up to 453 km (281 miles), which is among the longest in its class.
Kia EV2 First Edition (Source: Kia UK)
Kia’s EV5 beat out the Audi Q3 and Cupra Formentor VZ5 in the compact SUV category. Launched in December, the EV5 is about the size of the Sportage.
It’s available with front- and all-wheel-drive powertrains and offers a range of over 550 km (341 miles). Depending on the configuration, the EV5 can tow up to 1,800 kg (about 4,000 lbs).
Lastly, the Kia K4 Sportswagon, launched in May, outperformed the new Volkswagen ID.3 Neo and Cupra Born in the compact class.
Kia EV5 (Source: Kia)
In Europe, Kia offers a full lineup of all-electric vehicles, from the entry-level EV2 to the EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, three-row EV9, and PV5 van.
Sadly, Kia has no plans to sell the EV2 or EV5 in the US, but its popular EV3 ( see our review ) is now available. In 2024, the Kia EV3 won the Golden Steering Wheel award for “Best Car under €40,000.”
The 2027 Kia EV3 starts at $29,890, making it among the most affordable EVs in the US. It’s available in five trims and two battery packs.
The base Kia EV3 Light has a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range, while the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.

BYD is apologizing after a supplier error left some owners of its new full-size flagship SUV with the wrong wheels.
BYD apologizes for Great Tang wheel mix-up
The Great Tang, or Da Tang as it’s called in China, is the first flagship D-segment SUV under its Dynasty series, the largest and most luxurious SUV from the lineup.
After opening preorders at the Beijing Auto Show in April, BYD said the high-end SUV secured over 30,000 preorders in 24 hours. Two weeks later, preorders reached over 100,000.
By the time it went on sale in mid-June, over 150,000 buyers had preordered the Great Tang, marking a new record for a single BYD model.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
While it has been the top-selling pure electric large SUV for two months, with more than 10,000 sold since it hit the market, BYD issued an apology on November 11 for fitting the wrong front and rear wheel rims on some Great Tang models.
BYD apology for Great Tang wheel mix-up (Source: BYD/ Weibo)
The apology comes after several owners complained that the wheels were improperly installed on their vehicles.
BYD said the issue stemmed from a coding error by the wheel mesh assembly supplier, which led to incorrect assembly on some Great Tang vehicles.
BYD Great Tang (Datang) three-row electric SUV (Source: BYD)
The company said it “immediately” launched an investigation and corrected the issue so newly built vehicles will not be affected. In addition, the supplier introduced a new visual error-prevention mechanism to limit issues like this going forward.
BYD said the issue does not affect the vehicle’s handling or pose a safety risk during driving.
The company said owners can take affected vehicles to their local service center for a free inspection and professional wheel rim replacement. It’s also offering a replacement vehicle or compensation for transportation expenses.
BYD Great Tang interior (Source: Lu Tian)
Effective immediately, BYD said, the warranty on affected Great Tang vehicles will also be restarted.
The Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest Premium EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500).
All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries. While the base Premium model uses a 105.79 kWh battery, the Flagship EV trim uses a larger 130.15 kWh battery that delivers up to 590 miles (950 km) of CLTC range. It starts at 269,900 yuan ($40,000).
BYD Great Tang at a Flash Charger (Source: Lu Tian/ BYD)
The Great Tang is huge, measuring 5,263 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,800 mm high, with a wheelbase of 3,130 mm.
In comparison, that’s bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 and Kia EV9. It’s closer in size to the Li Auto L9.
Based on a 1,000V architecture with BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the electric SUV can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.
After launching in China, BYD executive vice president Stella Li said the flagship SUV will go on sale in Europe and other overseas markets by the end of 2026 or early 2027.

source_document.body:
260 Minerals employees inspecting core samples at the Bullabulling project. Credit: Kristie Batten.
Posted By: Colin McClelland November 11, 2026
Minerals 260 (ASX: MI6) has secured A$410 million (C$399 million) in bank debt for its Bullabulling gold project in Western Australia, with no requirement to lock in future gold prices.
ANZ, National Australia Bank and Société Générale have committed A$335 million for project financing and A$75 million for working capital. Together with equity and Franco-Nevada (TSX: FNV; NYSE: FNV) royalty funding, the package would cover development through first production, Minerals 260 said Wednesday.
Securing credit approval before completing the feasibility study reflects “the high quality, high margin and long-life aspects of Bullabulling,” Managing Director Luke McFadyen said in the release.
The backing advances a potential 150,000-oz.-a-year producer near Kalgoorlie, while leaving the construction decision and final loan conditions due early next year. Bullabulling could begin producing in the second half of 2028, Franco-Nevada said in September.
Early 2027 decision
Financing conditions include completing the definitive feasibility study, final due diligence, loan documents and an agreement with Franco-Nevada governing creditors’ rights. The first debt drawdown is expected late next year.
The project loan runs for seven years and working capital financing for four. Interest is less than three percentage points above Australia’s bank bill swap bid rate — equivalent to below about 8% annually using the current three-month benchmark. The company hasn’t disclosed the exact margin or benchmark term. Interest accrued during construction will be added to the debt.
BMO Capital Markets initiated coverage on Nov. 10 with an outperform rating and a A$1.75 share-price target. That is nearly twice Wednesday’s closing price of A88¢, a 3.5% gain, valuing the company at about A$2.25 billion. The shares have traded between about A29¢ and A$1 over the past year.
Royalty funding
Franco-Nevada agreed in September to provide another $170 million in royalty funding and buy $30 million of Minerals 260 shares. That brought its aggregate backing to $420 million and increased its gross royalty on Bullabulling to 3.9% from 2.45%.
July’s prefeasibility study envisaged annual output averaging about 150,000 oz. over the first decade and a 19-year operating life. The initial processing plant would handle 5 million tonnes annually, with provision for expansion, Franco-Nevada said.
Bullabulling, 65 km from Kalgoorlie, has 140 million indicated tonnes at 0.98 gram per tonne gold for 4.4 million oz., plus 51 million inferred tonnes at 1 gram gold for 1.7 million oz., according to a resource issued in July.

source_document.body:
Tesla has confirmed a new batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.
It’s a rare data point. Tesla doesn’t disclose Semi deliveries, and it claims its new Nevada factory can build 50,000 of them a year.
HMD Trucking’s 50 Semis
The post , published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, shows four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.
Hello Windy City Chicago’s first 50 Semis en route for delivery pic.twitter.com/75kig8yWsb — Tesla Semi (@tesla_semi) November 11, 2026
But the only 50-truck Semi order tied to Chicago belongs to HMD Trucking. The family-owned carrier was founded in Chicago in 1998, runs more than 650 trucks (almost all diesel), and ordered 50 Semis right after Tesla’s production event in September.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
HMD took its first truck on November 2 and says it’s the first Tesla Semi registered in Illinois. COO Michael Mahler said Tesla “has been transparent with us regarding the capabilities of Semi every step of the way.”
The company ran a Semi for more than 4,000 miles over the summer and averaged 1.74 kWh per mile, right in line with Tesla’s 1.7 kWh/mile claim. The first trucks will mostly handle local runs around Chicago, and HMD is installing its own chargers there since Tesla’s Megacharger network is still concentrated along the I-5 and I-10 corridors in the West.
Owner Henry Malukas told MotorTrend the deal is worth about $15 million. That’s roughly $300,000 per truck, in line with the ~$290,000 Long Range pricing we reported when the first truck came off the high-volume line and a long way from the $180,000 Tesla advertised in 2017.
Nobody knows where the Semi ramp is
Here’s the problem: it’s nearly impossible to tell how many Semis Tesla is actually building.
Tesla launched volume production at its Sparks, Nevada factory on September 24, after pushing the ramp out of 2025 . It says the 1.8 million sq ft plant is built for 50,000 trucks a year. But it never gave a ramp schedule, and its quarterly production and delivery reports only count “passenger vehicles sold to customers.” The Semi isn’t in there.
So we’re left with proxies. Tesla says its Semi fleet has over 98% uptime, without saying how big that fleet is. Before this year, the largest Semi fleet was PepsiCo’s, at 86 trucks in 2024. California’s truck voucher program received 965 Semi applications between January 2025 and February 2026, which points to real demand but says nothing about output.
The order book is the other clue. Einride ordered 500 Semis in August, WattEV has 370 on order, IMC Logistics wants 50 for California, and the ZET SCALE alliance picked Tesla as main supplier for 2,500 trucks. And now HMD’s 50 are rolling into Chicago, one of the first Semi fleets that will have to deal with a Midwest winter. Wisconsin’s Paper Transport has also been piloting a Semi in the Chicago market since the summer.
None of that adds up to a production rate, but it does look like Tesla is slowly ramping up deliveries.
Electrek’s Take
Tesla keeps the Semi numbers vague on purpose. It’s happy to talk about a 50,000-truck-a-year factory, and it posts hero shots when a batch ships, but it won’t give the one number that shows whether the factory is anywhere close to that.

The 50,000 figure is what makes the Semi look like a real business to investors instead of a niche program that took nine years to get going. Tesla has a long history of quoting capacity long before it reaches it, so we shouldn’t treat “built for 50,000” as anything more than a ceiling.
Our read: Tesla is still far from that 50,000 rate. Fifty trucks for one customer is 0.1% of a year at full capacity, and if Tesla were shipping in large volumes, a single 50-unit batch wouldn’t get its own post. But the ramp has clearly started, the order book is real, and it’s plausible Tesla gets into the thousands by the end of the year.
Good for HMD, too. A 650-truck diesel fleet in a cold market is exactly the kind of customer the Semi has to win. Malukas admitted “we don’t have real numbers yet” on savings, and HMD’s own blog is fairly sober about cost and winter range. Local routes, depot charging and a Chicago winter is the right way to find out. It all sounds plausible for the Tesla Semi.

Tesla launched volume production at its Sparks, Nevada factory on September 24, after pushing the ramp out of 2025 .

The order book is the other clue.
Einride ordered 500 Semis in August, WattEV has 370 on order, IMC Logistics wants 50 for California, and the ZET SCALE alliance picked Tesla as main supplier for 2,500 trucks.
Once the investment is justified, there will be customers and repeat customers.
